result.summary: Pausanias recounts the story of Ptolemy Philometor, his mother Cleopatra's intrigues, and the Athenian statues of Egyptian kings. He then turns to Lysimachus, Alexander's former armour-bearer, describing his wars with the Getae, his rebuilding of Ephesus, and his alleged violation of royal tombs in Epirus.

scenes.title: Philometor and Cleopatra's intrigues
scenes.summary: Cleopatra favours her younger son Alexander and has Philometor exiled. Alexander kills her, Philometor returns, crushes the Thebans, and is later honoured by Athens.
scenes.stakes: Philometor risks losing his kingdom and his life to his mother's plots.

scenes.title: Statues at Athens; Lysimachus introduced
scenes.summary: Pausanias notes the statues of Philip, Alexander and Lysimachus, tells how Lysimachus beat a lion, and comments on Thrace under the Romans.

scenes.title: Lysimachus against the Getae and Asia
scenes.summary: Lysimachus is defeated by Dromichetes and the Getae, makes peace, then crosses to Asia, overthrows Antigonus and founds a new Ephesus.
scenes.stakes: Lysimachus risks death or capture, and the loss of his son Agathocles.

scenes.title: Lysimachus in Epirus
scenes.summary: Lysimachus ravages Epirus. Pausanias doubts Hieronymus's claim that he desecrated the royal tombs.
scenes.stakes: Lysimachus's reputation is at stake against a hostile historian.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet meaning 'mother-loving', given ironically, as Pausanias says.

notable_quotes.reason: Opens with the irony of the name Philometor, 'mother-loving', for a king hated by his mother.

analysis.text: Pausanias digresses into the fortunes of the Hellenistic kings honoured at Athens, showing how power, flattery and family violence shaped their reputations.
Athens honoured foreign kings with statues for political usefulness, and Pausanias openly says so. He also tests his sources, such as Hieronymus, for bias.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias writes under Roman rule, noting that the Romans ignored parts of the Celtic land as worthless because of cold and poor soil.

language_notes.text: "Got his name in irony": Philometor means "mother-loving" in Greek, so the title is the opposite of the truth Pausanias describes.
"Obsequious" means eager to obey and please; Cleopatra expected a compliant son.
"Mutilated" refers to the eunuchs; she injured them herself to fake evidence of a plot.
Delphi and the Orchomenians (Orchomenus in Boeotia) were proverbially rich in treasure, so Theban wealth is measured against them.
"Meeting the common fate" is a euphemism for dying.
"Armour-bearer" was a close attendant who carried a warrior's arms; here a royal bodyguard.
"Contiguous" means bordering; Lysimachus got the Thracians nearest Macedonia.
Odrysæ were a powerful Thracian people; the Getæ lived north of Thrace, along the lower Danube.
Ister is the ancient Greek name for the lower Danube.
Phœnix of Colophon wrote choliambic (limping iambic) verse; his lament for Colophon's fall is the allusion here.
"Meddled with the tombs" is a mild expression for violating or opening the royal graves.
Calumny means a false and malicious charge.
Alexander here is Alexander the Molossian of Epirus, whose mother connected him to the Æacidæ, the line claiming descent from Achilles' grandfather Æacus.

context_notes.text: Pausanias is describing Ptolemaic Egypt, a Greek-ruled dynasty founded by Ptolemy son of Lagus, a general of Alexander the Great.
Thebes here is the Egyptian city, not the Greek one, and was a great religious and wealthy centre.
The lion story is a well-known anecdote about Lysimachus; Pausanias says he survived by defeating the beast.
The Celts were the Gauls and neighbouring peoples; the Romans conquered Thrace gradually, finally organising it as a province in AD 46.
Agathocles was Lysimachus' son and heir; he was later put to death on his father's orders.
Antigonus was the one-eyed Macedonian successor of Alexander; he fell at the battle of Ipsus in 301 BC.
Hieronymus of Cardia was a historian who served Alexander's successors and wrote a history of them, now lost.

literary_notes.text: The king's name, "mother-loving," contrasts bitterly with his mother's hatred.
Cleopatra is killed by the very son she raised to the throne, a fitting reversal for her scheming.
Pausanias breaks in with a personal aside, justifying a digression because these kings deserve more than a passing mention.
The Athenians are shown as flatterers whose honours follow usefulness rather than sincere goodwill.
Pausanias intrudes with a personal judgment, reasoning from absent evidence to date a poet.
Pausanias portrays Hieronymus as a biased source, undermining the accusation before weighing it.
The closing suggestion that Hieronymus had a grudge gently turns his own hostility against his reliability.
